title: Hyle's Self-Begetting: How the Enthumesis of Death Molded a Cosmos from Herself
arc: The teaching moves from the pre-cosmic question of how the two eternal substances exist, to the moment of mingling, to Hyle's solitary self-begetting of a counterfeit cosmos out of her own corrupt enthumesis, and ends with the archon's war-counsel and the First Man's answering descent into his god-garments — exposing self-love as a generative principle that can only produce, alone and out of itself, the foul multiplicity of evils against which Divine Truth must come down.
reading:
This chapter is a doctrinal treatment of how the present cosmos came to be, told from the side of darkness. It begins by asking the unanswerable question — how the things that exist from eternity exist, since no power of man can grasp them and there is no other power outside the two substances themselves. The frame is therefore the dualism of Light and Darkness as essentially-given: not produced, only mingled. The teaching's whole purpose is to show what kind of generation belongs to each pole, and especially to expose the generation that proceeds from the corrupt pole — the Enthumesis of Death, Hyle.

The pivot of the opening section is the sentence that survives intact: "From that time onward, the Light has been mingled with the Darkness, life with death." Everything before that statement is the eternal disposition of the two; everything after is the consequence. A king has descended (or attempted to ascend) against the Land of the Living Ones, hindrance has gone forth from the house of the Living against him, and from this collision the mingled state begins. That mingled state is the field in which Hyle's productive activity now operates, because Hyle is precisely the corrupt receptivity that becomes active once Light has been seized within her.

The body of the teaching is the great negative parallel to the Mother of Life. Where Divine Wisdom in her bringing-forth requires conjunction with Divine Good and brings forth a true offspring of life, Hyle "molded herself alone in her own land," "begot herself alone in her own begetting." This is the decisive correspondence: self-love can only generate from itself, without conjunction, and what it generates is therefore only itself dispersed into multiplicity. Hence the text's careful insistence — many creatures, "not in the likeness of one another," from the storehouses of her Deep. The proprium's productions have no real likeness because they have no shared interior; each is an isolated form of self-love, and so they are at war with one another from the start ("they kill out from one another, spreading out with one another"). Hatred and mutual destruction are not accidents in Hyle's world; they are the inner law of any cosmos generated by self-love alone.

What she begets are first the five corrupt elements — smoke, fire, wind, water, darkness — the dark counterpart of the Five Sons of the First Man. These are the natural-rational structure of the proprium: confused thought (smoke), corrupt love (fire as lust), disordered perception (wind), falsified truth (water), and the absence of light. From these she rises into trees and molds fruits while still standing fast in them: the perceptions and works of the corrupt natural mind, which then fall upon the earth and are nourished by the elements with concupiscence. The whole cosmos as we presently encounter it — its wild beasts, its dragons, its destroyers, its foul forms — is presented here as Hyle's self-portrait extruded into ultimates. Every form of the present world is, in this reading, a likeness of Hyle's solitary begetting, which is why it is "in foul forms" and ruled by hatred and killing.

The archon then enters as the executive of this state. His counsel surveys his cosmos and his powers, perceives the substance of the Light that has been seized within them, and ventures to make war against the lofty kingship — the King who dwells in the Land of Light. The teaching is showing how the proprium, having organized itself into a cosmos, then weaponizes that cosmos against heaven. Self-love does not merely exist; it conducts war, and the wisdom of darkness ("the wisdom of the…") is wholly oriented toward disturbing the Light.

Against this the closing movement turns. The Father of Greatness himself — though most of the sentence is lost — does not leave the situation to Hyle's terms. The First Man goes in unto his god-garments, the Lights, to speak with them, to be revealed to them, to teach them every work, to wear them, and to cast them one upon another against the enemy. These god-garments are the Five Sons: the five attributes of Divine Truth descending as the Living Soul, the true counter-pentad to Hyle's corrupt five elements. The teaching ends by setting the two armies against each other across the height of the earth, with all the archon's powers ranged on one side and Divine Truth, clothed in his Five, on the other; and the closing fragment — "there being no measure to her" — appears to register the unbounded scope of Hyle's productive corruption, the very feature that requires the Father's own descent to meet it.

Read as one argument, the teaching is a doctrine of two generations. True life is brought forth only by conjunction (Father and Mother of Life, Good with Truth); the proprium can only beget itself, alone, out of its own enthumesis, and what comes forth is therefore the mutual war of forms unlike one another. The cosmos around us is not neutral matter; it is the molded shape of the Enthumesis of Death, and the work of redemption is the First Man putting on his god-garments and walking down into precisely this molded land to recover the Light caught in it.

major_images.meaning: self-love as a generative principle that can only produce from itself without conjunction; the corrupt parallel to Mother of Life

major_images.image: Many creatures from the storehouses of her Deep, not in the likeness of one another, destroyers and dragons in foul forms, killing out from one another
major_images.meaning: the proprium's productions have no shared interior, so its cosmos is intrinsically a war of isolated self-loves

major_images.image: The five — smoke, fire, wind, water, darkness — rising into trees and molded fruits that fall upon the earth and are nourished with concupiscence
major_images.meaning: the corrupt five-fold structure of the natural-rational, the dark counterpart of the Five Sons, producing the perceptions and works of the unregenerate natural mind

major_images.meaning: the present cosmos as the mingled state in which Light is held captive within Hyle's self-generated forms
